en: Saṃyutta Nikāya 10.1 (SN 10.1, SN 235, PTS [1st ed. SN i 206, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 443) 1. Indaka Chapter: The Discourse to Indaka [The Buddha said: "Indaka, if one were to say: 'I do not see even a single dharma that, when developed and cultivated, leads to the abandoning of lust, hatred, and delusion,' this would be a false statement. For there is, Indaka, this dharma—namely, mindfulness directed to the body—which, when developed and cultivated, leads to the abandoning of lust, hatred, and delusion. "Indaka, if one were to say: 'I do not see even a single dharma that, when developed and cultivated, leads to the complete destruction of suffering,' this would be a false statement. For there is, Indaka, this dharma—namely, mindfulness directed to the body—which, when developed and cultivated, leads to the complete destruction of suffering. [Indaka asked: "Venerable sir, how is mindfulness directed to the body developed and cultivated so that it leads to the abandoning of lust, hatred, and delusion? [The Buddha replied: "Here, Indaka, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body as a body internally, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. He dwells contemplating the body as a body externally... He dwells contemplating the body as a body both internally and externally... He dwells contemplating the nature of arising in the body... He dwells contemplating the nature of passing away in the body... He dwells contemplating the nature of arising and passing away in the body—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. It is in this way, Indaka, that mindfulness directed to the body is developed and cultivated so that it leads to the abandoning of lust, hatred, and delusion. [Indaka asked: "Venerable sir, how is mindfulness directed to the body developed and cultivated so that it leads to the complete destruction of suffering? [The Buddha replied: "Here, Indaka, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body as a body internally, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. He dwells contemplating the body as a body externally... He dwells contemplating the body as a body both internally and externally... He dwells contemplating the nature of arising in the body... He dwells contemplating the nature of passing away in the body... He dwells contemplating the nature of arising and passing away in the body—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. It is in this way, Indaka, that mindfulness directed to the body is developed and cultivated so that it leads to the complete destruction of suffering. [Indaka said: "Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir! Just as if one were to set upright what had been overturned, or to reveal what was hidden, or to show the path to one who was lost, or to bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms, even so has the Dhamma been made clear by the Blessed One in many ways. I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Sangha of bhikkhus. May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts. [The Buddha said: "Indaka, you have been led by others; you have come under the influence of others. Therefore, Indaka, you should train yourself thus: 'I shall not abandon the Dhamma taught by the Tathāgata for the sake of another teacher. That is how you should train yourself. [Indaka said: "Venerable sir, I have been led by others; I have come under the influence of others. But I shall train myself thus: 'I shall not abandon the Dhamma taught by the Tathāgata for the sake of another teacher. [The Buddha said: "Indaka, you have been led by others; you have come under the influence of others. Therefore, Indaka, you should train yourself thus: 'I shall not abandon the training taught by the Tathāgata for the sake of another teacher. That is how you should train yourself. [Indaka said: "Venerable sir, I have been led by others; I have come under the influence of others. But I shall train myself thus: 'I shall not abandon the training taught by the Tathāgata for the sake of another teacher. [The Buddha said: "Indaka, you have been led by others; you have come under the influence of others. Therefore, Indaka, you should train yourself thus: 'I shall not abandon the Dhamma and the training taught by the Tathāgata for the sake of another teacher. That is how you should train yourself. [Indaka said: "Venerable sir, I have been led by others; I have come under the influence of others. But I shall train myself thus: 'I shall not abandon the Dhamma and the training taught by the Tathāgata for the sake of another teacher. [The Buddha said: "Indaka, you have been led by others; you have come under the influence of others. Therefore, Indaka, you should train yourself thus: 'I shall not abandon the Dhamma and the training taught by the Tathāgata for the sake of another teacher, nor shall I abandon the Dhamma and the training taught by the Tathāgata for the sake of gain, honor, or fame. That is how you should train yourself. [Indaka said: "Venerable sir, I have been led by others; I have come under the influence of others. But I shall train myself thus: 'I shall not abandon the Dhamma and the training taught by the Tathāgata for the sake of another teacher, nor shall I abandon the Dhamma and the training taught by the Tathāgata for the sake of gain, honor, or fame. [The Buddha said: "Indaka, you have been led by others; you have come under the influence of others. Therefore, Indaka, you should train yourself thus: 'I shall not abandon the Dhamma and the training taught by the Tathāgata for the sake of another teacher, nor shall I abandon the Dhamma and the training taught by the Tathāgata for the sake of gain, honor, or fame, nor shall I abandon the Dhamma and the training taught by the Tathāgata for the sake of my own life. That is how you should train yourself. [Indaka said: "Venerable sir, I have been led by others; I have come under the influence of others. But I shall train myself thus: 'I shall not abandon the Dhamma and the training taught by the Tathāgata for the sake of another teacher, nor shall I abandon the Dhamma and the training taught by the Tathāgata for the sake of gain, honor, or fame, nor shall I abandon the Dhamma and the training taught by the Tathāgata for the sake of my own life. [The Buddha said: "Indaka, you have been led by others; you have come under the influence of others. Therefore, Indaka, you should train yourself thus: 'I shall not abandon the Dhamma and the training taught by the Tathāgata for the sake of another teacher, nor shall I abandon the Dhamma and the training taught by the Tathāgata for the sake of gain, honor, or fame, nor shall I abandon the Dhamma and the training taught by the Tathāgata for the sake of my own life, nor shall I abandon the Dhamma and the training taught by the Tathāgata for the sake of my own pleasure. That is how you should train yourself. [Indaka said: "Venerable sir, I have been led by others; I have come under the influence of others. But I shall train myself thus: 'I shall not abandon the Dhamma and the training taught by the Tathāgata for the sake of another teacher, nor shall I abandon the Dhamma and the training taught by the Tathāgata for the sake of gain, honor, or fame, nor shall I abandon the Dhamma and the training taught by the Tathāgata for the sake of my own life, nor shall I abandon the Dhamma and the training taught by the Tathāgata for the sake of my own pleasure. [The Buddha said: "Indaka, you have been led by others; you have come under the influence of others. Therefore, Indaka, you should train yourself thus: 'I shall not abandon the Dhamma and the training taught by the Tathāgata for the sake of another teacher, nor shall I abandon the Dhamma and the training taught by the Tathāgata for the sake of gain, honor, or fame, nor shall I abandon the Dhamma and the training taught by the Tathāgata for the sake of my own life, nor shall I abandon the Dhamma and the training taught
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was staying at Rājagaha on Mount Indakūṭa, in the abode of the yakkha Indaka.
Then the yakkha Indaka approached the Blessed One; having approached, he addressed the Blessed One in verse:
“The Buddhas say that form is not the living being;
how then does this one find this body?
From where does this lump of bones and skin come?”
"How indeed does this one become attached within the womb?
"First there is the *kalala*;
from the *kalala* comes the *abbuda*."
From the abbuda the pesi is born;
from the pesi the ghana is produced;
from the ghana the limbs (pasākhā) arise.
The hair of the head, the body hair, and the nails;
and whatever food, drink, and nourishment his mother consumes.
By that he sustains himself there, the man dwelling within the mother’s womb.
*Saṁyutta Nikāya 10.2* (SN 10.2, SN 236, PTS [1st ed. SN i 206; PTS [2nd ed. SN i 444)
1. The Chapter on Indra:
The Discourse on the Name "Sakka" On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha on Vulture Peak Mountain.
Then a yakkha named Sakka approached the Blessed One; having approached, he addressed the Blessed One in verse:
"For you who have abandoned all fetters and are fully liberated;..."
“That is not good for a recluse,
that you should instruct another.
“In whatever way possible,” [he replied].
Association arises, O Sakyan;
a wise person ought not to feel compassion for such a one even in their mind.
If one instructs another with a mind full of faith,
one is not thereby fettered by that act.
“...that which is compassion and pity.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 10.3 (SN 10.3, SN 237, PTS [1st ed. SN i 207, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 445) 1.
Indaka Chapter (Indakavagga)
The Discourse on the Needle-Haired Yakkha On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Gayā, on the Hill of the Elephant’s Neck,
in the abode of the yakkha Sūciloma. Now at that time, the yakkha Kharo and the yakkha Sūciloma were passing by not far from the Blessed One.
Then the yakkha Kharo said this to the yakkha Sūciloma:
"This is a recluse. "He is not a recluse; he is a mere pseudo-recluse."
“Let me first find out whether he is a true ascetic or merely a pseudo-ascetic.
Then the yakkha Sūciloma approached the Blessed One; having approached, he thrust his body against the Blessed One’s body.
Thereupon, the Blessed One drew his body away.
Then the yakkha Sūciloma said this to the Blessed One:
“Are you afraid of me, ascetic?
“I am not afraid of you, friend.”
"Moreover, contact with you is evil.
"Ascetic, I will ask you a question.
If you do not answer me, I will either strike at your mind, or split your heart, or seize you by the feet and hurl you across the Ganges."
“Friend, I do not see anyone in the world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins,
its gods and humans, who could shake my mind, split my heart, or seize me by the feet and cast me across the Ganges.”
"Moreover, friend, ask whatever you doubt. (...
"From what source do lust and hatred arise?
From what are discontent, delight, and horripilation born?"
“From what do the mental thoughts arise,
like young birds releasing from a hawk?
“Lust and hatred have their source from this.”
Dislike, like, and horripilation are born from this;
mental thoughts arising from this dart forth like young birds from a hawk.
Born of craving, produced from oneself,
like the trunks of a banyan tree,
they are many and cling to sensual pleasures.
Like a *māluvā* creeper spreading through the forest,
those who understand its source dispel it; listen, O *yakkha*.
They cross this flood so difficult to cross,
which was never crossed before, for the sake of no further becoming.
1. The Chapter on Indra:
The Discourse to Maṇibhadda.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Magadhans at the Maṇimālika Shrine, in the abode of the yakkha Maṇibhadda.
Then the yakkha Maṇibhadda approached the Blessed One; having approached, he recited this verse in the presence of the Blessed One:
“Ever blessed is the one possessed of mindfulness;
the mindful one prospers in happiness.”
“For one possessed of mindfulness, tomorrow is better,
and they are released from enmity.
“For one possessed of mindfulness, there is always good fortune;”
One who possesses mindfulness thrives in happiness;
for one possessing mindfulness, it is better tomorrow,
as they are not released from enmity.
He whose mind delights in non-violence throughout the entire day and night,
who possesses loving-kindness toward all living beings—
“Nothing can contradict his truth. *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 10.5 (Indaka-vagga)
The Sānu Sutta.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now on that occasion a certain female lay follower had a son named Sānu who had been seized by a yakkha.
Then that female lay follower, lamenting at that time, spoke these verses:
"On the fourteenth, the fifteenth,
and on the eighth day of the fortnight;”
And they observe the Uposatha on the day of miracles, perfectly endowed with its eight factors.
"With those who lead the holy life,
the yakkhas do not play;
thus have I heard from the Arahants."
“Today I see them now;
the yakkhas are playing with the wind.
“On the fourteenth and the fifteenth,” [he said].
And the eighth day of the fortnight,
and the fortnight of miracles,
well-endowed with the eight factors.
Those who observe the Uposatha and live the holy life—
the Yakkhas do not sport with them.
Well done! You have heard what the Arahants have taught;
you should speak this word of the Yakkhas to Sānu when he has awakened.
Do not commit an evil deed,
whether openly or in secret.
And if you have committed an evil deed, [do not hide it].
Whether you will do it or are doing it,
there is no escape from suffering for you,
even if you flee after it has arisen.
“They weep for one who is dead,
or for one who is alive but not seen;
but seeing you alive, mother— ”
“Why do they weep for me, mother?
“They weep, my son, for one who is dead,
or for one who is alive but not seen.”
And even for one who, having abandoned sensual pleasures, returns here again—
it is for him too, my son, that they weep.
He is indeed dead though still living.
O dear one, having been pulled out from the pit of embers,
you wish to fall back into the embers.
O dear one, you have been pulled out from hell,
yet you wish to fall back into hell.
Run forward, O blessed one!
“Whom are we rebuking?
Having carried out goods from a burning house,
do you wish to burn them again?”

Saṃyutta Nikāya 10.6 (SN 10.6, SN 240, PTS [1st ed. SN i 209, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 451) 1. Indaka-vagga Piyaṅkara Sutta At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Sanctuary. At that time, the householder Piyaṅkara was residing in Rājagaha. He was wealthy, possessed of great riches, with vast assets and extensive property, with abundant gold and silver, abundant treasures and commodities, abundant wealth and grain, with many vehicles, many attendants, and many kinsmen and friends. Then, while the householder Piyaṅkara was seated in the inner apartments surrounded by his womenfolk, he spoke thus to them: “Ladies, it would be good if you were to go to the Blessed One and, having approached him, pay homage in my name with your heads at his feet, and inquire after his health, saying: ‘Venerable sir, is the Blessed One free from illness and affliction, and is he dwelling in comfort, vigorous, strong, and living in ease? “Yes, sir,” those women replied to the householder Piyaṅkara. Then, having dressed early in the morning and taken their fine jewelry, they went to the Blessed One. Having approached the Blessed One, they paid homage to him and sat down to one side. As they were sitting there, they said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, the householder Piyaṅkara pays homage to the Blessed One with his head at his feet and inquires after his health, saying: ‘Venerable sir, is the Blessed One free from illness and affliction, and is he dwelling in comfort, vigorous, strong, and living in ease? “Indeed, ladies, the Tathāgata is free from illness and affliction; he is dwelling in comfort, vigorous, strong, and living in ease. Then those women, having delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words, rose from their seats, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on their right, departed. Then, not long after those women had left, the householder Piyaṅkara fell ill. He was afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill. Then the householder Piyaṅkara addressed his kinsmen and friends: “Come, sirs, go to the Blessed One and, having approached him, pay homage in my name with your heads at his feet, and inquire after his health, saying: ‘Venerable sir, the householder Piyaṅkara pays homage to the Blessed One with his head at his feet and inquires after his health, saying: “Venerable sir, is the Blessed One free from illness and affliction, and is he dwelling in comfort, vigorous, strong, and living in ease? And say this: ‘Venerable sir, the householder Piyaṅkara is afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill. It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would visit the householder Piyaṅkara out of compassion. “Yes, sir,” those kinsmen and friends replied to the householder Piyaṅkara. Then, having approached the Blessed One, they paid homage to him and sat down to one side. As they were sitting there, they said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, the householder Piyaṅkara pays homage to the Blessed One with his head at his feet and inquires after his health, saying: ‘Venerable sir, is the Blessed One free from illness and affliction, and is he dwelling in comfort, vigorous, strong, and living in ease? Venerable sir, the householder Piyaṅkara is afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill. It would be good, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would visit the householder Piyaṅkara out of compassion. “Indeed, sirs, if the Tathāgata goes to the householder Piyaṅkara now, it would be for the latter’s harm and suffering. A second time and a third time, those kinsmen and friends repeated their request, and the Blessed One gave the same reply. Then the householder Piyaṅkara passed away. Not long after his death, the Blessed One dressed in the morning and, taking his bowl and robe, entered Rājagaha for alms. When he had walked for alms in Rājagaha and returned from his alms round, after his meal, he addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda, let us go to the householder Piyaṅkara’s residence. “Yes, venerable sir,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One, together with a large community of monks, went to the householder Piyaṅkara’s residence. At that time, the householder Piyaṅkara’s wife was seated in the inner apartments surrounded by her womenfolk. She saw the Blessed One approaching from afar. Seeing him, she spoke thus to those women: “Ladies, when the Blessed One comes here, pay homage to him with your heads at his feet in the name of the householder Piyaṅkara, and inquire after his health, saying: ‘Venerable sir, is the Blessed One free from illness and affliction, and is he dwelling in comfort, vigorous, strong, and living in ease? “Yes, madam,” those women replied to the householder Piyaṅkara’s wife. Then, as the Blessed One approached, they paid homage to him with their heads at his feet and sat down to one side. As they were sitting there, they said to the Blessed One:

“Venerable sir, the householder Piyaṅkara pays homage to the Blessed One with his head at his feet and inquires after his health, saying: ‘Venerable sir, is the Blessed One free from illness and affliction, and is he dwelling in comfort, vigorous, strong, and living in ease? “Indeed, ladies, the Tathāgata is free from illness and affliction; he is dwelling in comfort, vigorous, strong, and living in ease. Then the Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat. As he was sitting there, the Blessed One said to the Venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda, bring me some water from the well. “Yes, venerable sir,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One and brought some water from the well. Then the Blessed One washed his feet with that water. After washing his feet, the Blessed One set the water vessel down. Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda, go to the householder Piyaṅkara’s wife and say: ‘Sister, the Blessed One wishes to see you. “Yes, venerable sir,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One and went to the householder Piyaṅkara’s wife. Having approached her, he said: “Sister, the Blessed One wishes to see you. “Yes, venerable sir,” the householder Piyaṅkara’s wife replied to the Venerable Ānanda. Then, having risen from her seat and taken her fine jewelry, she went to the Blessed One. Having approached the Blessed One, she paid homage to him and sat down to one side. As she was sitting there, the Blessed One said to her: “Sister, where is the householder Piyaṅkara? “Venerable sir, the householder Piyaṅkara has passed away. Venerable sir, what is the destination, what is the rebirth, of the householder Piyaṅkara? “Sister, the householder Piyaṅkara was a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and assured of enlightenment. Then the householder Piyaṅkara’s wife, having heard that the Blessed One had declared the householder Piyaṅkara to be a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and assured of enlightenment, rose from her seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on her right, departed. Then the Blessed One, having instructed, inspired, and gladdened the Venerable Ānanda with a talk on the Dhamma, rose from his seat and departed. Then the Venerable Ānanda followed close behind the Blessed One. Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda, this householder Piyaṅkara was a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, and assured of enlightenment. Ānanda, if the householder Piyaṅkara had not passed away, he would have attained the fruit of once-returning within seven days. When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “
On one occasion the Venerable Anuruddha was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now on that occasion, as the night was drawing to a close, the Venerable Anuruddha rose and recited the verses of the Dhamma.
Then the yakkhinī Piyaṅkaramātā comforted her little son thus:
“Do not make a sound, Piyaṅkara;
the bhikkhu is reciting verses of the Dhamma.
Moreover, having understood even a single verse of the Dhamma,”
Let us practice so that it may lead to our welfare:
let us exercise restraint toward living beings,
and let us not speak falsehoods even when conscious of them.
"Let us train ourselves in virtue;
perhaps we may be released from the womb of a *pisāca*.
— *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 10.7 (SN 10.7, SN 241, PTS [1st ed. SN i 209, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 452)
1. The Chapter on Indra.
The Discourse to Punabbasu.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the Blessed One was instructing, exhorting, inspiring, and gladdening the bhikkhus with a Dhamma talk connected with Nibbāna.
Those bhikkhus listened to the Dhamma, having applied their hearts, having applied their minds, having directed their whole minds toward it, and lending an attentive ear.
Then the yakkhinī Punabbasumātā thus appeased her two children:
“Be silent, Uttarikā;
be silent, Punabbasu;
until I [have spoken] to the Best of Buddhas.”
I shall hear the Dhamma from the Teacher.
The Blessed One has spoken of Nibbāna,
the liberation from all fetters.
And there is in me an exceeding measure of fondness for this Dhamma;
one’s own son is dear in the world.
One's own husband is dear in the world;
yet the seeking of the path of Dhamma is even dearer to me than he.
For neither a son nor even a husband can liberate one from suffering as effectively as hearing the true Dhamma.
He liberates living beings from suffering in this world that is beset by misery and joined with aging and death.
I wish to hear that Dhamma which you have fully awakened to for the sake of liberation from aging and death.
“Be silent, Punabbasu.
“Mother, I shall not speak;
Uttarā remains silent.”
Pay close attention to the Dhamma alone;
hearing the true Dhamma is blissful,
for it leads to the full understanding of the true Dhamma.
Alas, we undergo suffering!
He is the dispeller of darkness for gods and humans who are utterly bewildered.
“The Buddha, whose body is his last,
the Visionary, teaches the Dhamma.
“Truly, it is good that he is called ‘the Wise One’ (Paṇḍita).”
A son has been born to me from my breast;
this son of mine cherishes the pure Dhamma of the Best of Buddhas.
Punabbasu, may you be happy;
today I have emerged.
The Noble Truths have been seen.
“Let Uttara also hear from me.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 10.8 (Indaka-vagga)
The Sudatta Sutta.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Cool Grove.
Now at that time the householder Anāthapiṇḍika had arrived at Rājagaha on some business or other.
The householder Anāthapiṇḍika heard:
“It is said that a Buddha has appeared in the world.
At that very moment, he desired to go and see the Blessed One. Then, this thought occurred to the householder Anāthapiṇḍika:
“It is not the right time today to approach the Blessed One for a visit.
Tomorrow, at the proper time, I shall go to see the Blessed One. With mindfulness directed toward the Buddha, he lay down.
During the night, he indeed arose three times, thinking that it was dawn.
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika approached the gate of the charnel ground.
Non-human beings opened the gate for him.

As the householder Anāthapiṇḍika was departing from the city, the light vanished, darkness appeared, and fear, trepidation, and horripilation arose within him; he then desired to turn back right there.
Then the yakkha Sivaka, having vanished, raised his voice:
"A hundred elephants, a hundred horses,
and a hundred chariots drawn by mules!"
A hundred thousand maidens,
adorned with jeweled earrings,
[are not worth a sixteenth part] of a single stride forward.
They are not worth a sixteenth part of it.
Come forward, householder!
Come forward, householder!
“Advancing is better for you than retreating.
Then, for the householder Anāthapiṇḍika, the darkness vanished and light appeared; whatever fear, trepidation, and horripilation he had experienced subsided.
A second time, the light of the householder Anāthapiṇḍika vanished, darkness appeared, and fear, trepidation, and horripilation arose; he desired to turn back from that very spot.
A second time, the yakkha Sivaka, having become invisible, made this sound heard:
"A hundred elephants, a hundred horses..."
... [as before] ... they do not equal even a sixteenth part of it.
Come forward, householder!
"Come forward, householder!
It is better for you to come forward than to go back."
Then, for the householder Anāthapiṇḍika, the darkness disappeared and light appeared; the fear, trepidation, and horripilation that had arisen subsided.

For a third time, however, the light for the householder Anāthapiṇḍika disappeared and darkness appeared; fear, trepidation, and horripilation arose, and he again desired to turn back from that very spot.
For a third time, the yakkha Sivaka, having vanished, raised his voice:
“A hundred elephants, a hundred horses,
… [as above] … do not equal even a sixteenth part of it.”
Come forward, householder,
come forward, householder;
it is better for you to come forward.
“...there is no turning back.
Then, for the householder Anāthapiṇḍika, the darkness vanished and light appeared; whatever fear, trepidation, and horripilation he had experienced subsided.
Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika approached the Cool Grove where the Blessed One was staying.
Now at that time, the Blessed One, having risen at the time of dawn during the latter part of the night, was walking back and forth in the open air.
The Blessed One saw the householder Anāthapiṇḍika coming from afar.
Seeing him, he descended from his walk and sat down on the prepared seat.
Having sat down, the Blessed One said this to the householder Anāthapiṇḍika:
“Come, Sudatta.

Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika, thinking, “The Blessed One addresses me by name,” was thrilled and elated; right there, he prostrated with his head at the Blessed One’s feet and said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, I hope the Blessed One has slept well?
“The brahmin who has attained final Nibbāna always sleeps in happiness.”
He who is not smeared by sensual pleasures,
become cool and free from acquisitions,
having severed all attachments—
Having removed the piercing dart from his heart,
he who is at peace dwells happily,
having attained tranquility with his mind.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 10.9 (SN 10.9, SN 243, PTS [1st ed. SN i 212, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 458) 1. Indaka Chapter The First Discourse on the White Cloth At Sāvatthī. There, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, suppose there were a white cloth, clean and pure, and a skilled dyer were to dip it into a dye-vat of blue, yellow, red, or crimson; it would take the color well, become thoroughly saturated, and appear beautiful. So too, bhikkhus, if a bhikkhu possesses four qualities, he is one who will quickly attain final knowledge (*parinibbāna*). What four? (1) Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is possessed of faith; he has faith in the Tathāgata’s enlightenment thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. (2) He is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of good conduct and resort, seeing danger in the slightest fault; having undertaken the training rules, he trains in them. (3) He is learned; he has retained in mind what he has heard from the Teacher or his disciples—the discourses, mixed prose and verse, expositions, verses, inspired utterances, legends, birth stories, marvelous accounts, and answers to questions—and by doing so, he is a bearer of the Dhamma, a bearer of the Vinaya, and a bearer of the Teacher’s instructions. (4) He gains at will, without trouble or difficulty, the four jhānas that constitute the higher mind and are pleasant dwellings in this very life. Possessing these four qualities, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu is one who will quickly attain final knowledge. This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Fortunate One, the Teacher, further said this: “One endowed with faith, virtuous, Learned, and possessing the four jhānas— Such a bhikkhu, diligent and wise, Will soon attain final peace.”
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Now at that time, the bhikkhunī Sukkā, surrounded by a large assembly, was teaching the Dhamma.
Then a yakkha who had full confidence in the bhikkhunī Sukkā approached from street to street and crossroads to crossroads in Rājagaha, and on that occasion recited these verses: [The verses follow.]
“What have the people of Rājagaha done to me that they lie down as if drunk on honey—
those who do not wait upon the Pure One?”
Descending toward the deathless state—
which is indeed irresistible and possesses an invigorating essence that requires no seasoning.
"The wise, I think, drink [of it], just as travelers [drink] from a cloud.
—Saṁyutta Nikāya 10.10 (SN 10.10, SN 244, PTS (1st ed. SN i 212; PTS (2nd ed. SN i 459)
1. The Chapter on Indra.
The Second Discourse to Sukkā.
At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Now at that time, a certain lay follower gave food to the bhikkhunī Sukkā.
Then a yakkha who had full confidence in the bhikkhunī Sukkā, having approached from street to street and from crossroads to crossroads in Rājagaha, on that occasion recited this verse:
“Truly, she has produced much merit!”
“Truly wise is this lay follower,
who gave food to her who is liberated from all fetters.”
Saṃyutta Nikāya 10.11 (SN 10.11, SN 245, PTS [1st ed. SN i 213, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 460) 1. Indaka Chapter The Discourse on Tattered Rags (Cīrāsutta)
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Now on that occasion a certain lay follower gave a robe to the bhikkhunī Cīrā.
Then a yakkha who was deeply devoted to the bhikkhunī Cīrā, having approached from street to street and from crossroads to crossroads in Rājagaha, recited this verse at that time:
“Truly, he has produced much merit!
Truly, this lay follower is wise!”
And he who gave a robe to Cīra for the sake of liberation from all bonds.
*Saṁyutta Nikāya 10.12* (SN 10.12, SN 246, PTS [1st ed. SN i 213, PTS [2nd ed. SN i 460)
1. The Chapter on Indra:
The Discourse to Āḷavaka.
Thus have I heard—
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Āḷavī in the abode of the yakkha Āḷavaka.
Then the yakkha Āḷavaka approached the Blessed One and, having approached, said this to the Blessed One:
“Come out, ascetic!”
“Excellent, friend,” the Blessed One said, and he went out.
“Enter, ascetic,” [the other said].
“Excellent, friend,” the Blessed One said, and he entered.
A second time, the yakkha Āḷavaka said this to the Blessed One:
“Come out, ascetic!
“Very well, friend,” the Blessed One replied, and he came out.
“Enter, ascetic.
“Very well, friend,” the Blessed One entered.
For a third time, the yakkha Āḷavaka said this to the Blessed One:
“Come out, ascetic!
“Very well, friend,” the Blessed One replied, and he came out.
“Enter, ascetic! he was told.
“Very well, friend,” the Blessed One said, and he entered.
For a fourth time, the yakkha Āḷavaka spoke thus to the Blessed One:
“Come out, ascetic!”
“Friend, I will not go out;
do whatever you must do.
“I shall ask you a question, ascetic.”
“If you do not answer me, I will either strike at your mind, or split your heart, or seize you by the feet and hurl you across the Ganges.
“Friend, I do not see anyone in the world with its gods, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins,
its devas and humans, who could strike at my mind, split my heart, or seize me by the feet and hurl me across the Ganges.”
“...one might throw it across the Ganges.
Moreover, friend, ask whatever you doubt.
“What indeed is the supreme wealth for a person here?”
What well-practiced thing brings happiness?
What indeed is the sweetest of tastes?
How does one live that they call the best life?
“Faith is the supreme wealth of a person here;
the Dhamma well-practiced brings happiness;
truth indeed is the sweetest of tastes.”
“Life lived by wisdom, they say, is the best.
“How indeed does one cross the flood?
How indeed does one cross the ocean?”
“How does one transcend suffering?
How is one purified?
“Through faith one crosses the flood;”
By heedfulness one crosses the ocean;
by energy one overcomes suffering;
by wisdom one is purified.”
“How does one obtain wisdom?
How does one find wealth?
How does one attain fame?”
How does one bind friends?
How does one go from this world to the next,
and not grieve after passing away?
“Having faith in the Dhamma of the Arahants for the attainment of Nibbāna,
one gains wisdom through the desire to learn.”
The diligent and discerning person,
who acts appropriately, bears the burden,
and exerts effort, finds wealth.
Through truth one attains fame;
by giving, one binds friends;
from this world one goes to the next world.
Thus, having passed away, one does not grieve—
this person who possesses these four qualities,
being faithful, though seeking a household life.
Truth, Dharma, fortitude, and generosity—
he indeed does not grieve after passing away.
Come now, ask others as well.
"Among the many ascetics and brahmins,
if there exists here any truth or generosity greater than patience," so he said.
“How indeed shall I now question the many recluses and brahmins,
when it is I myself who today understand?”
That which is for the sake of the future life—
for my own benefit indeed, the Buddha has come to Āḷavī to dwell.
Today I understand where what is given bears great fruit;
such as I am, I shall wander.
From village to village, from town to town,
he paid homage to the Fully Awakened One and to the sublime nature of the Dhamma.
The first chapter, the Indaka Chapter.
Its summary verse:
Indaka, Sakka, and Sūci.
Maṇibhadda and Sānu;
Piyaṅkara, Punabbasu, and Sudatta,
along with the two Sukkas and Cīra Āḷavī— these are the twelve.
The Connected Discourses on Yakkhas are complete.
